opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the really exciting thing about Haiku is that it's our smallest, fastest, cheapest model, and it's still doing really well on SWE-bench Verified, somewhere around 40%. Not that long ago, that would have been state of the art from the biggest frontier models. So a model you can run cheaply and quickly is now doing real, agentic software engineering: navigating a repo, figuring out what's wrong, writing a fix, and checking it.

What I find most interesting is what that means for builders. When a smaller model can do this, you can run a lot more attempts in parallel. You can put it in loops where it tries something, runs the tests, and iterates. You can also use it in places where latency and cost used to rule out an agent entirely. A lot of agent design so far has been limited by "this is too slow" or "this is too expensive to run at scale," and Haiku pushes those limits back a lot.

It also says something about the trend. Capabilities that start out in the largest models keep filtering down into smaller ones pretty quickly. For people building on these models, a good bet is to design for where things are going, not just for what works today, because the cheap model a few months from now will probably handle the task you're designing around.

r001.rationale: The response says Haiku is Anthropic’s smallest model and describes it doing agentic software engineering on SWE-bench: navigating a repository, finding the problem, writing a fix, and checking it.

fable-5.1.text:
What really excites me about Haiku's SWE-bench number is less the number itself and more what it tells you about the trajectory. Haiku is our smallest, cheapest, fastest model, and it's scoring in the low forties on SWE-bench Verified, which is higher than where the original Claude 3.5 Sonnet was just a few months earlier, and well above a lot of frontier models from a year ago. So you've got this little model doing agentic coding tasks that, not long ago, we considered state of the art for the biggest models anyone had.

And SWE-bench is a hard benchmark to game. These are real GitHub issues from real repositories. The model has to read the issue, navigate a codebase it's never seen, figure out which files matter, write a fix, and then that fix has to actually pass the hidden tests. It's not a single-shot "write me a function" problem. It requires the model to keep its bearings over many steps, use tools, recover from mistakes. That's a very different kind of capability than just knowing a lot of trivia.

The reason that matters practically is cost and latency. If you're building an agent that's running dozens or hundreds of tool calls, the economics of doing that with a frontier model can be rough. Having a model at Haiku's price point that can genuinely do the work opens up a whole class of applications. You can imagine a system where a cheap model handles most of the routine edits and only escalates to Sonnet when it gets stuck. Or you just run many more attempts in parallel and pick the best one.

The other thing I'd point to is what it suggests about where the field is going. A lot of the gains here came from better training, better data, and better understanding of how to teach the model to behave in an agentic loop, not just from scale. When small models improve this fast on a task that's this close to real engineering work, it tells me we're still pretty early. The frontier keeps moving, but the floor is rising with it, and the floor rising is what actually changes what people can build.

r001.rationale: It describes Haiku as Anthropic’s smallest model and says it handles difficult, multi-step agentic coding tasks involving real repository issues, fixes, and hidden tests.
